structure.title: Sections I–III · Take inventory of the mind
structure.text: Hume separates vivid impressions from the fainter ideas available in thought. An unfamiliar philosophical term now faces a practical challenge. From what experience could somebody have acquired the idea it claims to express?

structure.title: Sections IV–VII · Why expect the next ball to move?
structure.text: Repeated sequences let us predict causes and effects, but past conjunctions contain no proof that nature will continue in the same course. Hume asks what habit contributes to belief and where the impression behind the idea of necessity might be found.

structure.title: Sections VIII–XII · Try the account on matters people fight over
structure.text: Human action, animal learning, testimony about miracles and arguments for providence bring the earlier tests into disputed territory. The closing discussion asks what kind of scepticism an inquirer can actually sustain while living an ordinary life.

people.name: Custom
people.text: After watching one event regularly follow another, the observer comes to anticipate the second on seeing the first. Hume locates much of daily confidence in that transition, including confidence in cases no one could demonstrate beforehand.

people.name: Testimony
people.text: A witness's word ordinarily has weight because experience has taught us something about the reliability of witnesses. Hume uses the same basis to ask how much weight an extraordinary report actually deserves.

context.title: Relations of ideas and matters of fact
context.text: Denying an arithmetical truth produces a contradiction. Imagining tomorrow's sun failing to rise does not. Hume uses the distinction to isolate the sort of reasoning on which almost every practical decision depends.

notice.text: Put a first-time observer beside the billiard table.
notice.why: Without a history of collisions, which features of the first ball reveal the future movement of the second? Hume strips away familiarity so the contribution of experience becomes unexpectedly visible.

notice.text: Notice how often the animal gets there too.
notice.why: An animal learns what follows a signal without assembling a philosophical proof. The example gives Hume a demanding comparison for any proposed explanation of what humans do in the same situation.

opening: The sun has risen every morning you remember. That gives you confidence it will rise tomorrow, but Hume asks what justifies the step from what has happened to what must happen next. The answer proves harder than ordinary life allows us to notice. His investigation follows the difficulty into cause and effect, freedom, and reports of miracles. Calm, lucid sentences uncover how much of our reasoning rests on habits we cannot establish by the kind of proof we thought we possessed.
